latin.1753: I. Plerique Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Calvino, & aliis qui cum eo in Religionis negotio sentiunt, tribuere solent quod ab homine tollant liberum arbitrium, eumque omni libertate in agendo spolient, aut saltem doceant in eo liberum Arbitrium per peccatum penitus amissum & extinctum fuisse. Istud videre est apud Bailium Jesuitam in Catechesi quam refutat Rivetus in summa Controversiarum Tract. 4. quaest. 4. Ubi disputat contra Reformatos, quasi liberum hominis arbitrium simpliciter negarent: & apud Martinum Becanum Jesuitam alterum qui dicit Lutheranos & Calvinistas affirmare per peccatum primi parentis penitus sublatum esse liberum arbitrium. In summa Theol. Scholast. Tract. 1. cap. 2. quaest. 9.
latin.1754: II. Sed constans est Reformatorum omnium sententia liberum arbitrium simpliciter consideratum, & secundum propriam naturam atque essentiam, esse aliquid quod a creatura rationali separari non potest: adeoque libere agendi facultatem ab homine per peccatum prorsus sublatam non fuisse: imo hominem per peccatum corruptum non minus libere agere quae agit, quam agebat ante peccatum: ac seu sibi relictus peccato indulgeat, id plane summa cum libertate facere; sive per gratiam motus & excitatus meliori vitae studeat, actus illius quoque liberos esse, neque per gratiae Dei efficaciam quicquam libertati voluntatis ejus praejudicari.
latin.1755: III. Inter eos etiam constat liberum illud arbitrium quod ab homine inseparabile est, non esse actum, aut habitum aliquem, sed potius quandam animae facultatem: neque tamen isto nomine designari facultatem quandam, quae sit a mente & voluntate distincta; sed liberum arbitrium homini convenire, quatenus intellectu & voluntate praeditus est.
latin.1756: IV. Verum non explicant omnes eodem modo qua in re sita sit libertas, ratione cujus homo liber in agendo dicitur, & a qua denominatur liberum ejus arbitrium. Et primo quidem ex Reformatis non pauci, libertatem illam cujus respectu homo dicitur esse liberi arbitrii, nec servituti, nec necessitati simpliciter opponi docent, sed potius coactioni. Ac plerumque loquuntur quasi coactio sola libertatem perimeret, & libertatem describunt immunitatem a coactione.
latin.1757: V. Nec tamen eorum mens est quaecunque sponte, & non coacta agunt, agentia esse libera. Agnoscunt enim bruta sponte agere, & ea nihilominus libertate spoliant. Itaque ad libertatem praeterea requirunt, ut qui agit non simpliciter naturae impulsu ducatur; sed ex consilio & ratione agat. Adeoque ex eorum mente, plena libertatis definitio erit, siquis dicat illam esse immunitatem a coactione in eo qui agit ex rationis judicio.
latin.1758: VI. Sic Marcus Wendelinus Christianae Theologiae lib. 1. cap. 5. in explicatione Theseos 18. liberum arbitrium definit, Voluntatis affectionem, qua proprio suo motu, absque coactione, eligit, vel repudiat rem ab intellectu monstratam. Et huic quoque similis est definitio Zachariae Ursini, Est itaque, inquit, liberum arbitrium facultas, seu potentia volendi, aut nolendi, seu eligendi, aut repudiandi objectum ab intellectu monstratum, proprio motu, sine coactione. In explicationibus Catecheticis, parte 1. quaest. 8. num. 1.
latin.1759: VII. Ex hac vero sententia sequitur libertatem proprie consistere in lubentia illa, qua voluntas intellectus judicium sequitur, non vero in aliqua voluntatis indifferentia, aut potestate quadam ad opposita, sine qua consistere potest voluntatis libertas; quamvis revera voluntas ad multos suos actus indifferenter se habeat, ut docet idem Wendelinus loco modo citato. Ubi postquam tradidit jam allatam definitionem liberi arbitrii, subjungit, Hoc in genere ad arbitrii libertatem sufficit: quod enim addunt nonnulli, per arbitrium liberum voluntatem sua natura manere idoneam ad oppositum, seu diversum eligendum, vel actionem suspendendam; ad liberum arbitrium in genere non pertinet. Quia libertas arbitrii consistit quoque sine indifferentia ad utrumque oppositum, quam contrarietatis libertatem appellant. Adeoque libertas quoque est, quae ad oppositorum alterutrum determinata est: qualis in beatis, qui libere agunt bene, ita ut per confirmationem in bono non possint male agere. Imo ne contradictionis quidem libertas simpliciter ad arbitrii libertatem est necessaria: quia libere Deum laudant Beati, qui tamen non possunt non laudare.
latin.1760: VIII. Quamvis igitur ille, & qui cum eo sentiunt, agnoscant discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe ad quosdam voluntatem determinatam esse, aliorum vero respectu natura sua manere idoneam ad opposita; censent tamen voluntatem, tam horum quam illorum respectu, liberam dici debere, & tam hos quam illos libere a voluntate prodire & elici. Ac proinde distinguunt quidem inter voluntarium simpliciter, & illud quod fit ex electione: sed inter voluntarium & liberum non distinguunt. Nam utrumque volunt aeque late patere, & quicquid voluntarium est, hoc ipso esse liberum. Nec ullam necessitatem quae voluntarii naturam non evertat, libertatis naturam evertere existimant. Adeoque quamvis Deus per naturam bonus sit, docent tamen illum esse libere bonum, quoniam non coacte, sed voluntarie bonus est. Sicuti videre est apud Zachariam Ursinum loco jam allegato. Liberum, inquit, vocatur ἑκούσιον, hoc est, spontaneum: quod opponitur ἀκουσίῳ, hoc est, involuntario, & coacto: non autem ἀναγκαίῳ, seu necessario. Potest enim ἑκούσιον consistere cum ἀναγκαίῳ, sed non cum ἀκουσίῳ, ut Deus & sancti Angeli ἀναγκαίως, hoc est, necessario sunt boni: non tamen ἀκουσίως, hoc est, coacte, sed liberrime: quia principium suae bonitatis habent in seipsis, liberam voluntatem.
latin.1761: IX. Alii vero diserte & distincte affirmant, libertatem illam a qua homo liber in agendo dicitur, non esse immunitatem a sola coactione, quae est necessitas quam infert vis agentis externi, contra inclinationem illius quod cogi dicitur: sed libertatem illam opponi praeterea necessitati naturali, sive determinationi per naturam ad unum. Porro necessitas illa, quam naturalem vocant, a materia juxta ipsos oritur, idque duplici modo. Vel enim actio externa non dependet ab ulla actione interna a qua imperetur: sed posita facultate, & objecto materiali extrinsecus admoto, non potest non exerceri actio, & quidem talis, tantaque. Cui necessitati subjiciuntur, quaecunque sensu & ratione carent. Vel pendet quidem actio externa ab internae imperio, ut & suspendi possit, & non eodem modo semper fieri, sed tamen non nisi a re aliqua materiali determinatio oritur: sicuti contingit in brutis, quorum actiones externae a sensu pendent atque imperantur, & magnam varietatem, etiam circa unum & idem objectum admittunt, prout sensus eorum varie, tum interne, tum externe afficiuntur; sed ipsi eorum sensus ab objecto aliquo materiali semper moventur & determinantur. Homo vero ab utraque ista necessitatis specie immunis est. Nec enim in actibus illis, quorum respectu dicitur liberi esse arbitrii, a materia externe admota, aut etiam a solo materiali sensu in agendo determinatur. Sed cum sit agens intellectualis, agit atque appetit ex judicio atque imperio rationis.
latin.1762: X. Qua in re libertatem arbitrii constituunt. Idque quoniam illi qui ex judicio rationis agunt finis notitiam habent, eumque sibi praestituunt, & ad eum actiones suas dirigunt atque accommodant: & ita sunt quodammodo actionum suarum Domini. Cum contra res inanimae, & animalia bruta quae solo sensu ducuntur, finem suum non cognoscant; ideoque ad eum seipsa non referant, sed duntaxat ad illum tendant instar mancipiorum, imperata quidem facientium, cur vero imperentur, aut quorsum ignorantium. Neque tam propter finem agunt, quam ad finem ab agente superiore aguntur. Adde quod brutorum sensus & appetitus rebus materialibus astrictus est; hominum vero voluntas, cum sequatur ductum mentis & rationis, quae pro objecto habet non tantum sensibilia, sed etiam intelligibilia, non solum praesentia, sed etiam futura, versatur circa omnia bonorum genera, modos atque gradus, nec ullis, ut sic dicam, limitibus includitur: Unde nascitur maxima appetitionum electionumque necnon actionum externarum varietas.
latin.1763: XI. Quae latius diducta videre licet apud Josuam Placeum ante paucos annos in Academia Salmuriensi Professorem, tractatu de libero hominis Arbitrio. Ubi sic concludit ea quae pluribus ante hac de re disseruit. In eo igitur consistit naturalis voluntatis libertas, quod cum a coactione, & necessitate materiae, & rerum sensibilium sit libera, tam immaterialia quam materialia, tam intelligibilia quam sensibilia, tam futura quam praesentia, tam honesta quam utilia, aut jucunda, horumque contraria, omnes adeo bonorum & malorum ordines, gradus, relationes pro objecto habere possit omni loco & tempore, finem ultimum, fines intermedios, ad eosque conducentia media eligere potest pro arbitrio, hoc est, mentis practicae judicio, sine qua ne rationalis quidem est, nedum libera. Et postea repetit ex sua sententia non omnem necessitatem cum voluntate, id est, cum libertate arbitrii pugnare, sed eam duntaxat quae vel a coactione est, vel a materia sine sensu, vel a sensu sine ratione. Item, libertatem sitam esse in immunitate a triplici necessitate, coactionis nempe, determinationis a materia, & determinationis a sensu.
latin.1764: XII. Sed sunt qui ad libertatem actionum humanarum putant non sufficere immunitatem a coactione, & a necessitate determinationis a materia vel a sensu; sed libertatem illam praeterea excludere necessitatem quamlibet naturalem, etiamsi a materia, vel a sensu non oriatur. Nec etiam, ut actio libera sit, satis esse existimant, ut homo quovis modo ex judicio rationis agat; ad hoc etiam requiri tale judicium quod sit conclusio cujusdam deliberationis, & consultationis; adeoque illa solum libere a nobis fieri, de quibus consultare & deliberare licet. Ac proinde cum sint quidam voluntatis nostrae actus ad quos per naturam determinata est, & circa quos nemo unquam consultat atque deliberat, qualis est actus ille quo beati esse volumus, & nolumus esse miseri, circa hos voluntatem liberam esse non sentiunt: nec etiam ad modum causae liberae se habere, respectu motuum illorum qui in voluntate subito excitantur, ex perturbatione aliqua vehementi, priusquam mens nostra seipsam colligere potuerit, & deliberationem aliquam instituere. Unde est quod distinguunt inter liberum & voluntarium, & statuunt voluntarium latius patere quam liberum: cum voluntarium omne liberum non sit.
latin.1765: XIII. Haec est doctrina Andreae Riveti olim in Academia Leydensi Professoris Summae Controversiarum tract. 4. quaest. 3. Libertatis rationem agnoscimus, inquit, consistere non posse, non solum cum coactione proprie dicta, sed etiam cum necessitate naturali, qua agens ad unum natura determinatum est; nec sufficere ad libertatem si homo sponte aliquid faciat, quod etiam causis naturalibus competit, sed necessariam esse deliberationem praeviam, & rationis judicium, quae locum non habent ubi est determinatio ex naturae necessitate. Et postea, Nos, inquit, in libertate haec tria distinguimus, quibus liberi arbitrii naturam per se explicamus. 1. Ut sit libertas in subjecto, nempe in voluntate, quae ex principio suo interno, sine discursu & consilio, agit semper sponte citra coactionem; sed cum consilio & deliberatione libere citra necessitatem. Sine prima libertate a coactione destruitur natura voluntatis, cui necessitas imponitur ut cogi non possit in actu suo, ut vocant, elicito. Sine deliberatione autem ex indifferentia intellectus, libere velle non potest, nempe si natura ad unum determinata esset. Et propterea liberum arbitrium cum Thoma dicit esse vim electivam. Et cum Bellarmino agnoscit ad essentiam liberi arbitrii pertinere, ut quis habeat optionem diversarum rerum, & electio fiat cum pleno atque perfecto rationis judicio.
latin.1766: XIV. Similis est hac in parte Doctrina Mosis Amyraldi nuper in Academia Salmuriensi Professoris Tractatu de libero hominis arbitrio, p. 61. & seqq. Ubi primo distinguit duplicem voluntatis motionem. Unam quae non est sejuncta quidem ab ea cognitione quae a ratione ducit originem, sed est istiusmodi tamen ut cognitio ex qua nascitur ac efflorescit, non sit ipsa orta ex praevia consultatione: alteram quae non modo conjuncta est cum aliqua cognitione, sed nascitur ex ea notitia quam προβούλευσις, i. e. consultatio antecessit, & quae nihil aliud est quam Conclusio quae ex deliberatione conficitur, consideratis, scilicet, atque comparatis inter se pluribus objectis, aut uno & eodem objecto spectato diversimode, adeo ut mens aliquandiu hinc & illinc rationum librata ponderibus, tandem in unam partem inclinetur. Deinde observat illam voluntatis motionem, quae nullam mentis consultationem & deliberationem sequitur, adhuc duplicem esse, nimirum voluntatem per unam in finem, id est, beatitudinem & felicitatem ipsam ferri; per alteram in media quae ad finem istum ducere existimantur.
latin.1767: XV. Postea vero neutram istarum motionum ad liberum arbitrium pertinere ostendit. Non priorem, quia liberum arbitrium est id quod Aristoteles προαίρεσιν appellavit. Jam vero, inquit, προαίρεσιν omnem antecedit aliqua προβούλευσις. Nemo autem de extremo illo fine consultat, sed fertur in eum non necessario duntaxat, sed etiam ἀπροβουλεύτως. Non etiam superiorem, quia etsi motus iste a superiori differat, est etiam cum eo aeque ἀπροβούλευτος. Siquidem usque adeo subitus est, usque adeo velociter, vel ex perturbatione aliqua ortus, vel ex ingentis alicujus & improvisi atque inopinati objecti praesentia natus erumpit, ut omnem consultationem antevertat. Unde colligit motum ejusmodi esse quidem ἑκούσιον, id est, spontaneum & voluntarium, non autem προαιρετικόν, id est, liberum atque electivum. Ac propterea recte dici solere primos passionum nostrarum impetus non esse in nostra potestate; quoniam ea sola sunt in nostra potestate de quibus consilium capimus, an sint a nobis, vel usurpanda, vel omittenda: ac proinde quae omnem deliberationem praecurrunt, illa in potestate nostra esse non arbitramur. Unde tandem concludit pag. 65. Restat ergo ut ad arbitrium nostrum pertinere putentur ea de quibus deliberare possumus, utque illa itidem ex arbitrio nostro libero profecta esse dicamus de quibus ita deliberavimus, ut deliberationem & consultationem secuta sit appetitio: qua in re τὴν προαίρεσιν, jam saepe sitam esse diximus.
latin.1768: XVI. Sed praeter necessitatem quae est a coactione, a materia, vel a sensu, aut a quavis alia naturae determinatione, quaedam necessitas est quae concipitur oriri ab aliqua causa externa, velut ab ipso Deo, sic facultatem ipsam movente atque impellente, ut veram imponat agendi necessitatem, id est, ab agente tollat potestatem aliter agendi; licet qui agit supponatur agere sponte, & non invitus. Quam necessitatem Scholae motivam atque impulsivam vocant. Non desunt autem inter Reformatos, qui hanc quoque necessitatem cum humana libertate pugnare existiment, quique putent cum ea consistere non posse ullam proprie dictam necessitatem, quae in Scholis appellatur necessitas consequentis, opposite ad necessitatem quae consequentiae dicitur.
latin.1769: XVII. Haec est sententia Gulielmi Amesii olim in Academia Franekerana Theologi, Nos, inquit, concedimus liberum arbitrium, in eo quod agit liberum esse ab omni necessitate, ut proprie non possit necessario agere quoad exercitium sui actus, quamvis respectu divinae ordinationis certo & infallibiliter agat. In Bell. Enervato tom. 4. lib. 4. cap. 1.
latin.1770: XVIII. Idem quoque sentit Rob. Baronius olim in Academia Abredonensi Professor in Metaphysica sua generali ad Theologiae usum accommodata, ubi inter alia multa haec duo asserit, Primo voluntatem in suis actionibus eliciendis non teneri, vel constringi necessitate absolute dicta, quam appellant necessitatem consequentis. Deinde voluntatem, etiam hominis lapsi, nulla necessitate motiva, vel impulsiva teneri respectu Dei. Ille etiam, inquit, hominibus liberum arbitrium dedit, & per consequens non tollit totaliter eam facultatem, ei imponendo necessitatem, aut per decretum suum aeternum, aut per temporariam motionem, & inflexionem. Sect. 12. Disp. 1. de libertate Arbitrii num. 17.
latin.1771: XIX. Ut autem quid mihi quoque videtur aperiam, existimo primam sententiam quae libertatem definit immunitatem a coactione in eo qui agit ex judicio rationis, reipsa non differre a secunda sententia, quae libertatem opponit non tantum coactioni, sed etiam necessitati quae a materia vel a sensu oritur, quam alii Physicam necessitatem vocant. Quandoquidem enim statuit immunitatem a coactione non esse dignam nomine libertatis, nisi in eo qui ratione utitur; evidenter supponit ad libertatem requiri, ut agens rationis judicium sequatur, non vero a materia, vel a sensu determinetur. Adeoque haec secunda sententia a priori non differt, nisi quod proponitur distinctius & explicatius.
latin.1772: XX. In utraque autem istud incommodi est quod omnino confundunt liberum & voluntarium, & statuunt omnes actus voluntatis liberos esse. Nam juxta sensum communem hominum, & receptum loquendi usum, istud solum liberum nobis esse dicitur, quod in nostra potestate est, quod potest aliter se habere, & de quo nobis consultare & deliberare licet. Jam vero, ut supra ostendimus, sunt quidam voluntatis actus, ad quos per naturam sic determinata est, ut nullo modo possint aliter se habere, & de quibus nulla potest institui deliberatio. Adde quod omnes actus qui a nobis libere procedunt possunt praeceptis quibusdam subjacere, & lege aliqua divina, vel humana mandari, sive prohiberi. Istud autem nullo modo convenit iis actibus circa quos voluntas plane immutabiliter se habet, ita ut in nullo statu potuerit, vel possit unquam aliter agere. Denique cum illi quibuscum nobis res est, fateantur & agnoscant magnum discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe quosdam sic esse in nostra potestate, ut de iis possimus consultare & deliberare; illosque pro vario mentis practicae judicio, vel facere, vel omittere, aut etiam contrarium agere; aliorum vero plane diversam esse rationem; cur nolunt res natura distinctas, distinctis quoque vocibus signare, & juxta usum in Scholis receptum illis quidem liberi, his vero voluntarii nomen appropriare? cum sapientis sit sine necessitate a communi loquendi modo non recedere.
latin.1773: XXI. Caeterum inter Doctos illos viros qui liberum & voluntarium confundere videntur, nonnulli sunt qui monent libertatem voluntatis, sive liberum Arbitrium duplici modo sumi, late, scilicet, & stricte. Libertas voluntatis in genere, sive late sumpta, juxta ipsos, nihil aliud est quam τὸ ἑκούσιον νοητικόν, spontaneum intellectuale, id est, spontaneum praeeunte intellectus lumine, vel judicio. Adeoque in hoc proprie consistit generalis ista voluntatis libertas, quod voluntas hactenus Dominium sui actus habeat, ut nequaquam cogi possit, sed pro libito, ex certa ratione, consideratione, aut judicio, sese moveat, & cohibeat, agat, aut non agat.
latin.1774: XXII. Haec est illa libertas, quam ex eorum sententia, voluntas in omnibus suis actionibus exercet, idque non tantum quum versatur circa media ad finem spectantia, aut ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, sed etiam, quum versatur circa ipsum finem. Ac proinde ipsa necessitas quae voluntatis naturam sequitur, eique consentanea est, & per quam determinata est ad summum finem prosequendum, hanc voluntatis libertatem minime evertit, aut minuit.
latin.1775: XXIII. Strictius vero usurpata libertas, sive liberum arbitrium restringitur, ipsis fatentibus ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, & versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, circa ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & recte ab Aristotele definitur spontaneum ex praevia deliberatione ortum, sive Deliberativa appetitio eorum quae sunt in nostra potestate. Quo in sensu liberi actus dicuntur qui sunt mere contingentes, & qui a nobis pro arbitrio fieri possunt, aut non fieri. Eoque respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, neque aliter voluntas libera est quam quatenus est indifferens, nempe, cum possit circa idem objectum agere, vel non agere, & cum possit tam illud, quam aliud, aut ejus oppositum eligere. Et hoc sensu Deus libere se non amat, quia naturae necessitate seipsum vult & amat; nec etiam homo libere vult esse foelix, & non vult esse miser, quia sic vult & non aliter per naturalem quandam necessitatem.
latin.1776: XXIV. Haec est doctrina Johannis Strangii, S. S. Theologiae Doctoris & Professoris primarii in Academia Glasguensi, Tractatu de voluntate & actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3. cap. 14. Ubi postquam haec quae diximus exposuit & latius diduxit, dicit se non negare vocem liberi arbitrii stricto illo sensu recte usurpari, quanquam in alio & latiori sensu affirmet omnes voluntatis actiones esse liberas. Et simili quoque modo liberum arbitrium distinguit Celeberrimus Alexander Morus, De Gratia & libero Arbitrio Disp. 1. Thesi 28. Ubi duas proponit definitiones, unam liberi arbitrii latius accepti, alteram vero liberi arbitrii stricte sumpti. Juxta priorem notionem liberum arbitrium ab ipso describitur, Dos intelligentis naturae maxime propria qua nihil vult, aut aversatur, nisi quod esse bonum, aut malum intellexit. Juxta vero posteriorem, voluntas quatenus media post consultationem ab intellectu monstrata eligit.

sections.title: Roman teachers charge Calvin and the Reformed with taking free choice away from man
sections.pass_a: Most Doctors of the Roman Church are wont to attribute to Calvin, and to others who agree with him in the business of Religion, that they take away free choice from man, and strip him of all liberty in acting, or at least teach that in him free Choice was wholly lost and extinguished through sin. This may be seen in Bailius the Jesuit in the Catechism which Rivet refutes in the summary of Controversies Tract. 4. quest. 4. Where he disputes against the Reformed, as though they simply denied the free choice of man: and in Martin Becanus another Jesuit who says that Lutherans and Calvinists affirm that through the sin of the first parent free choice was wholly taken away. In the summa of Scholastic Theology Tract. 1. chap. 2. quest. 9.
pass_b: Most teachers of the Roman Church commonly accuse Calvin and those who share his religious position of removing free choice from man and stripping him of any freedom in what he does. At the least, they say, these men teach that sin destroyed free choice in man altogether.

One example is the Jesuit Bailly, in the catechism that Rivet answers in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 4). There Bailly argues against the Reformed as if they flatly denied that man has free choice.

Another is the Jesuit Martin Becanus. In his Summa of Scholastic Theology (treatise 1, chapter 2, question 9) he says that Lutherans and Calvinists hold that the sin of our first parent completely did away with free choice.

choices.why: Le Blanc's whole locus turns on the faculty, not on a state of liberty; 'free choice' keeps the scholastic term without the later connotations of 'free will' as a separate power.

notes: Bailius (Bailly) the Jesuit, Catechism, answered by Rivet, Summa Controversiarum, tract. 4, q. 4; Martin Becanus, Summa theologiae scholasticae, tract. 1, cap. 2, q. 9.

sections.title: The Reformed hold that free choice belongs to the rational creature and was not lost by sin
sections.pass_a: But it is the constant opinion of all the Reformed that free choice considered simply, and according to its proper nature and essence, is something which cannot be separated from a rational creature: and so the faculty of acting freely was not altogether taken away from man through sin: indeed that man corrupted through sin acts no less freely the things he does, than he acted before sin: and whether, left to himself, he indulges sin, he does this plainly with the greatest liberty; or, moved and stirred up by grace, he strives after a better life, his acts also are free, and nothing is prejudiced to the liberty of his will through the efficacy of the grace of God.
pass_b: Yet all the Reformed consistently hold that free choice, taken simply and in its own nature and essence, cannot be separated from a rational creature. So sin did not wholly remove man's power to act freely.

Indeed, man corrupted by sin acts no less freely in what he does than he did before sin. If he is left to himself and gives way to sin, he does it with complete freedom. If grace moves and rouses him to pursue a better life, those acts are free too, and the efficacy of God's grace takes nothing away from his will's freedom.

choices.english: takes nothing away from his will's freedom
choices.why: Praejudicare here means to impair or prejudice a right; 'take away from' gives the sense without legal jargon.

sections.title: Free choice is not an act or habit but a faculty, belonging to man as he has intellect and will
sections.pass_a: Among them it is also agreed that that free choice which is inseparable from man, is not an act, or some habit, but rather a certain faculty of the soul: and yet that by that name is not designated some faculty which is distinct from mind & will; but that free choice belongs to man, inasmuch as he is endowed with intellect and will.
pass_b: They also agree that the free choice which cannot be separated from man is not an act or a habit. It is rather a faculty of the soul.
Even so, the name does not mean some faculty distinct from mind and will. Man has free choice because he has an intellect and a will.

choices.why: Habitus is the scholastic term for a settled disposition, as distinct from a single act or a faculty; 'habit' is the standard English term.

sections.title: Many Reformed oppose liberty only to compulsion and define it as freedom from compulsion
sections.pass_a: But not all explain in the same way in what thing liberty is situated, by reason of which man is said to be free in acting, and from which his choice is called free. And first indeed not a few of the Reformed teach that that liberty in respect of which man is said to be of free choice, is opposed neither to servitude, nor simply to necessity, but rather to coaction. And for the most part they speak as though coaction alone destroyed liberty, and they describe liberty as immunity from coaction.
pass_b: They do not all explain in the same way what the freedom consists in that makes man free in acting and gives his choice the name free.

To begin with, a good many of the Reformed teach that the freedom by which man is said to have free choice is not set against bondage, or against necessity as such, but against compulsion. They mostly talk as if compulsion were the only thing that destroys freedom, and they describe freedom as exemption from compulsion.

choices.why: Coactio is force applied against an agent's own inclination; 'compulsion' renders the technical sense.

sections.title: They add that the agent must act from counsel and reason, not mere impulse of nature
sections.pass_a: Nor yet is their mind that whatever things act spontaneously, and not coerced, are free agents. For they acknowledge that brutes act spontaneously, and nevertheless they strip them of liberty. Therefore they require besides for liberty, that he who acts be not simply led by the impulse of nature; but act from counsel and reason. And so according to their mind, the full definition of liberty will be, if one says that it is immunity from coaction in one who acts from the judgement of reason.
pass_b: They do not mean, though, that everything that acts of its own accord and without compulsion acts freely. They grant that animals act of their own accord, yet they deny them freedom.

So for freedom they also require that the agent not simply be driven by nature's impulse but act from deliberation and reason. On their view, then, the full definition of freedom is exemption from compulsion in an agent who acts on the judgement of reason.

choices.why: Consilium here is the weighing of a course of action, not advice from another; 'deliberation' gives the sense.

sections.title: Wendelin and Ursinus define free choice as choosing without compulsion what the intellect shows
sections.pass_a: So Marcus Wendelin Christian Theology book 1. chap. 5. in explaining Thesis 18. defines free choice, An affection of the will, by which by its own motion, without coaction, it chooses, or rejects a thing shown by the intellect. And to this also similar is the definition of Zacharias Ursinus, Free choice therefore, he says, is a faculty, or power of willing, or not willing, or of choosing, or rejecting an object shown by the intellect, by its own motion, without coaction. In the Catechetical explanations, part 1. quest. 8. num. 1.
pass_b: Thus Marcus Wendelin, explaining thesis 18 in his Christian Theology (book 1, chapter 5), defines free choice as "a disposition of the will by which, moving itself and without compulsion, it chooses or rejects what the intellect sets before it."

Zacharias Ursinus gives a similar definition in his Catechetical Explanations (part 1, question 8, number 1): "Free choice, then, is a faculty or power of willing or not willing, of choosing or rejecting, an object that the intellect sets before it, by its own movement and without compulsion."

lemmas.gloss: that the intellect sets before it

choices.why: The phrase stresses that the motion starts from the will itself; 'moving itself' and 'by its own movement' keep the point in both definitions.

notes: Marcus Friedrich Wendelin, Christianae theologiae libri duo, book 1, chapter 5, thesis 18; Zacharias Ursinus, Explicationes catecheticae, part 1, question 8, number 1.

sections.title: On this view freedom lies in willingness, not indifference; Wendelin says the blessed praise God freely though they cannot not praise
sections.pass_a: From this opinion it follows that liberty properly consists in that willingness, by which the will follows the judgement of the intellect, not in any indifference of the will, or some power to opposites, without which the liberty of the will can stand; although in fact the will holds itself indifferently towards many of its acts, as the same Wendelin teaches in the place just cited. Where after he has given the definition of free choice already brought forward, he adds, This in general suffices for liberty of choice: for what some add, that by free choice the will remains by its nature apt for the opposite, or for choosing something different, or suspending action; does not pertain to free choice in general. Because liberty of choice consists also without indifference to either opposite, which they call liberty of contrariety. And so that also is liberty, which is determined to one of opposites: such as in the blessed, who freely act well, so that through confirmation in good they cannot act ill. Indeed not even liberty of contradiction is simply necessary to liberty of choice: because the Blessed freely praise God, who yet cannot not praise.
pass_b: It follows from this view that freedom properly lies in the willingness with which the will follows the intellect's judgement. It does not lie in any indifference of the will or any power for opposites, since the will's freedom can exist without these, even though in fact the will is indifferent toward many of its acts. Wendelin teaches this in the same passage.

After giving the definition quoted above, he adds: "This is enough, in general, for freedom of choice. Some add that through free choice the will by its nature stays able to choose the opposite or something else, or to hold back from acting. That does not belong to free choice in general.

"For freedom of choice also exists without indifference to either of two opposites, which they call the freedom of contrariety. So it is also freedom when the will is fixed on one of two opposites. That is how it is with the blessed: they do good freely, yet being confirmed in good they cannot do evil.
"Indeed, not even the freedom of contradiction is strictly necessary to freedom of choice. The blessed praise God freely, and yet they cannot fail to praise him."

choices.why: In the schools indifferentia is the will's openness to either of two options; the technical term is kept and explained by the context.

notes: Liberty of contrariety is the power to choose either of two contraries (this or its opposite); liberty of contradiction is the power to act or not act.

sections.title: Wendelin and Ursinus make every voluntary act free, so that God is freely good because not by compulsion
sections.pass_a: Although therefore he, and those who agree with him, acknowledge that there is a difference between acts of the will, namely that to some the will is determined, but in respect of others it remains by its nature apt for opposites; they nevertheless judge that the will, as much in respect of these as of those, ought to be called free, and that as well these as those proceed and are elicited freely from the will. And therefore they distinguish indeed between the voluntary simply, and that which is done from election: but between the voluntary and the free they do not distinguish. For they will both to extend equally widely, and whatever is voluntary, by this very fact to be free. Nor do they think that any necessity which does not overturn the nature of the voluntary, overturns the nature of liberty. And so although God is good by nature, they teach yet that he is freely good, since he is good not by coaction, but voluntarily. As may be seen in Zacharias Ursinus in the place already alleged. Free, he says, is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous: which is opposed to akousion, that is, involuntary, and coerced: but not to anankaion, or necessary. For hekousion can stand with anankaion, but not with akousion, as God and the holy Angels are anankaios, that is, necessarily good: yet not akousios, that is, by coaction, but most freely: because they have the principle of their goodness in themselves, a free will.
pass_b: He and those who agree with him admit a difference among the will's acts: the will is fixed on some of them, while toward others it stays by nature able to go either way. Still they hold that the will should be called free with respect to both kinds, and that both kinds come freely from the will.

So they do distinguish between what is simply voluntary and what comes from choice, but they draw no line between the voluntary and the free. They want the two to cover the same ground, so that whatever is voluntary is free for that very reason. They do not think any necessity destroys the nature of freedom unless it also destroys the nature of the voluntary.

They therefore teach that God, though good by nature, is freely good, because his goodness is not forced but willed. Ursinus says this in the passage cited above: "What is free is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous. It is the opposite of akousion, the involuntary and forced, but not of anankaion, the necessary.

"Hekousion can go with anankaion, but not with akousion. God and the holy angels are good anankaios, that is, necessarily, yet not akousios, that is, under force; they are good most freely, because the source of their goodness is in themselves, a free will."

choices.why: Electio in this locus is the act of choosing after deliberation (Aristotle's prohairesis); 'choice' keeps it parallel with 'free choice'.

notes: Ursinus' Greek terms are transliterated in Pass B: hekousion (voluntary), akousion (involuntary), anankaion (necessary).

sections.title: Others oppose liberty also to natural necessity, determination by matter or by sense
sections.pass_a: But others expressly and distinctly affirm, that that liberty from which man is called free in acting, is not immunity from coaction alone, which is the necessity which the force of an external agent brings in, against the inclination of that which is said to be coerced: but that that liberty is opposed besides to natural necessity, or determination by nature to one. Further that necessity, which they call natural, arises according to them from matter, and that in a twofold manner. For either the external action does not depend on any internal action by which it is commanded: but the faculty being posited, and the material object applied from without, the action cannot not be exercised, and indeed such, and so great. To which necessity are subjected, whatever lack sense and reason. Or the external action depends indeed on the command of an internal one, so that it can also be suspended, and not always be done in the same way, but yet the determination arises only from some material thing: as happens in brutes, whose external actions depend on and are commanded by sense, and admit great variety, even about one and the same object, according as their senses are variously affected, both internally, and externally; but their senses themselves are always moved and determined by some material object. But man is immune from both those kinds of necessity. For in those acts, in respect of which he is said to be of free choice, he is not determined in acting by matter applied externally, or even by material sense alone. But since he is an intellectual agent, he acts and desires from the judgement and command of reason.
pass_b: Others state plainly and precisely that the freedom by which man is called free in acting is not exemption from compulsion alone, compulsion being the necessity imposed by an outside agent's force against the inclination of the thing compelled. That freedom, they say, is also opposed to natural necessity, that is, to being fixed by nature on one outcome.

This natural necessity, on their account, comes from matter, and in two ways. In one, the outward action does not depend on any inner act that commands it. Once the faculty is there and a material object is brought to it from outside, the action must take place, and with just this character and this strength. Everything without sense and reason is subject to this necessity.

In the other, the outward action does depend on an inner command, so that it can be held back and need not always happen the same way, yet what settles it comes only from something material. That is the case with animals. Their outward actions depend on sense and are directed by it, and they vary a great deal even toward one and the same object as their senses are affected in different ways, inwardly and outwardly. But their senses themselves are always moved and settled by some material object.

Man is free of both kinds of necessity. In the acts for which he is said to have free choice, he is not settled in acting by matter brought to him from outside, or even by material sense alone. Being an intellectual agent, he acts and desires on the judgement and command of reason.

lemmas.gloss: being fixed by nature on one outcome

choices.why: The scholastic phrase means a power that can produce only one effect; 'fixed on one outcome' renders it in plain words.

sections.title: Hence rational agents are masters of their actions, unlike things moved only by sense
sections.pass_a: In which thing they place the liberty of choice. And that because those who act from the judgement of reason have knowledge of the end, and set it before themselves, and direct and accommodate their actions to it: and so are in a manner Masters of their actions. Whereas on the contrary inanimate things, and brute animals which are led by sense alone, do not know their end; and therefore do not refer themselves to it, but only tend to it like slaves, doing indeed what is commanded, but ignorant why it is commanded, or to what purpose. Nor do they so much act for an end, as they are acted to an end by a superior agent. Add that the sense and appetite of brutes is bound to material things; but the will of men, since it follows the leading of mind and reason, which has for object not only sensible things, but also intelligible, not only present, but also future, is occupied about all kinds, modes and degrees of goods, nor is it enclosed, so to speak, by any limits: Whence arises the greatest variety of appetitions and elections and also of external actions.
pass_b: This is where they locate freedom of choice. Those who act on reason's judgement know their end, set it before themselves, and direct and fit their actions to it, so that in a sense they are masters of what they do.

Lifeless things and animals that are led by sense alone, by contrast, do not know their end. So they do not direct themselves to it but only move toward it like slaves, who carry out orders without knowing why they are given or what they are for. They do not so much act for an end as get moved toward an end by a higher agent.

Besides, the sense and appetite of animals are tied to material things. Human will follows the lead of mind and reason, whose objects are not only things of sense but things of the intellect, not only present things but future ones. It ranges over every kind, mode and degree of good and is shut in, so to speak, by no limits. From this comes the great variety in what men desire and choose, and also in their outward actions.

choices.why: The plural abstract nouns name acts of desiring and choosing; turning them into verbs reads more naturally.

sections.title: Josué de la Place: freedom is exemption from compulsion, from matter, and from sense
sections.pass_a: Which may be seen drawn out more widely in Josue de la Place a few years ago Professor in the Academy of Saumur, in the treatise on the free choice of man. Where he thus concludes the things which he discussed at more length before on this matter. In this therefore consists the natural liberty of the will, that since it is free from coaction, and from the necessity of matter, and of sensible things, it can have for object as well immaterial as material things, as well intelligible as sensible, as well future as present, as well honest as useful, or pleasant, and their contraries, indeed all orders, degrees, relations of goods and evils in every place & time, and can choose the ultimate end, intermediate ends, and the means conducing to them at its discretion, that is, by the judgement of the practical mind, without which it is not even rational, much less free. And afterwards he repeats from his own opinion that not every necessity conflicts with the will, that is, with liberty of choice, but only that which is either from coaction, or from matter without sense, or from sense without reason. Likewise, that liberty is situated in immunity from a threefold necessity, namely of coaction, of determination by matter, & of determination by sense.
pass_b: This is set out more fully by Josué de la Place, professor at the Academy of Saumur a few years ago, in his treatise On Man's Free Choice. There he sums up what he had argued at length before: "The natural freedom of the will consists in this. Being free of compulsion and of the necessity of matter and of things of sense, it can take as its object, in any place and at any time, things immaterial as well as material, of the intellect as well as of sense, future as well as present, honourable as well as useful or pleasant, and their opposites, in short every order, degree and relation of goods and evils.

"It can choose the final end, the intermediate ends and the means that lead to them as it judges fit, that is, by the judgement of the practical mind. Without that judgement it would not even be rational, let alone free."

Later he repeats, as his own view, that not every necessity clashes with the will, meaning with freedom of choice, but only the necessity that comes from compulsion, or from matter without sense, or from sense without reason. Likewise he says freedom lies in exemption from three necessities: compulsion, being settled by matter, and being settled by sense.

lemmas.gloss: the judgement of the practical mind

choices.why: Honestum is the morally good as distinct from the useful and the pleasant; 'honourable' keeps the classical triad.

notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus), professor at Saumur, treatise De libero hominis arbitrio.

sections.title: Some exclude all natural necessity and require deliberation, distinguishing the voluntary from the free
sections.pass_a: But there are those who think that for the liberty of human actions immunity from coaction does not suffice, and from the necessity of determination by matter or by sense; but that that liberty besides excludes any natural necessity whatever, even if it does not arise from matter, or from sense. Nor do they think it enough, that an action be free, that man act in any way from the judgement of reason; for this is also required such a judgement as is the conclusion of some deliberation, and consultation; and so only those things are done freely by us, about which it is permitted to consult and deliberate. And therefore since there are certain acts of our will to which it is determined by nature, and about which no one ever consults and deliberates, such as is that act by which we will to be blessed, and will not to be miserable, about these they do not think the will is free: nor also that it behaves after the manner of a free cause, in respect of those motions which are suddenly stirred up in the will, from some vehement perturbation, before our mind could collect itself, and set up some deliberation. Whence it is that they distinguish between the free and the voluntary, and state that the voluntary extends more widely than the free: since not every voluntary thing is free.
pass_b: Some, however, think that exemption from compulsion and from being settled by matter or sense is not enough for human actions to be free. In their view freedom also rules out every kind of natural necessity, even one that does not come from matter or sense.

Nor do they think it enough for a free action that a man act on reason's judgement in any way at all. The judgement must be the conclusion of some deliberation and weighing. Only those things are done freely by us, then, about which we can take counsel and deliberate.

Now there are some acts of our will to which it is fixed by nature and about which no one ever deliberates, such as the act by which we want to be happy and do not want to be miserable. They do not hold that the will is free in these. Nor do they think it acts as a free cause in the impulses that rise in it suddenly from some violent disturbance before our mind can collect itself and begin to deliberate.
That is why they distinguish the free from the voluntary and hold that the voluntary is the wider class, since not everything voluntary is free.

choices.why: Beatus here names natural happiness as the will's last end, the classic example of a necessary volition; 'happy' fits the paired 'miserable'.

sections.title: Rivet: freedom excludes natural necessity and requires prior deliberation
sections.pass_a: This is the doctrine of Andrew Rivet formerly Professor in the Academy of Leiden Summary of Controversies tract. 4. quest. 3. We acknowledge, he says, that the nature of liberty cannot consist, not only with coaction properly so called, but also with natural necessity, by which an agent is determined by nature to one; nor that it suffices for liberty if a man do something spontaneously, which belongs also to natural causes, but that previous deliberation is necessary, and the judgement of reason, which have no place where there is determination from the necessity of nature. And afterwards, We, he says, distinguish these three things in liberty, by which we explain the nature of free choice in itself. 1. That liberty be in the subject, namely in the will, which from its internal principle, without discourse & counsel, acts always spontaneously without coaction; but with counsel & deliberation freely without necessity. Without the first liberty from coaction the nature of the will is destroyed, on which the necessity is imposed that it cannot be coerced in its act, as they call it, elicited. But without deliberation from the indifference of the intellect, it cannot will freely, namely if it were determined by nature to one. And therefore with Thomas he says free choice is an elective power. And with Bellarmine he acknowledges that it pertains to the essence of free choice, that one have the option of different things, and that election be made with full and perfect judgement of reason.
pass_b: This is the teaching of Andrew Rivet, formerly professor at the Academy of Leiden, in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 3): "We acknowledge that the nature of freedom cannot coexist with compulsion in the proper sense, nor with natural necessity either, by which an agent is fixed by nature on one outcome. It is not enough for freedom that a man does something of his own accord, since natural causes do that too. Prior deliberation and a judgement of reason are required, and these have no place where nature's necessity settles the act."

Later he says: "We distinguish three points in freedom, by which we explain the nature of free choice in itself. 1. Freedom is in a subject, namely the will. Acting from its own inner principle without reasoning or deliberation, the will always acts of its own accord and without compulsion; acting with counsel and deliberation, it acts freely and without necessity.

"Without the first freedom, from compulsion, the nature of the will is destroyed, for necessity is laid on the will that it cannot be forced in what they call its elicited act. Without deliberation arising from the intellect's indifference, it cannot will freely, since it would then be fixed by nature on one outcome."

So with Thomas he calls free choice an elective power. And with Bellarmine he grants that it belongs to the essence of free choice that one has the option between different things and that the choice is made with a full and complete judgement of reason.

choices.term: cui necessitas imponitur ut cogi non possit
choices.english: necessity is laid on the will that it cannot be forced
choices.why: Rivet's point is that being unforceable is itself necessary to the will's nature; the English keeps his paradoxical wording.
rejected: the will is compelled not to be forced

notes: Andrew Rivet, Summa controversiarum, tract. 4, q. 3. An elicited act is one the will itself produces, as distinct from an act it commands another faculty to do.

sections.title: Amyraut distinguishes motions of the will that follow deliberation from those that do not
sections.pass_a: Similar in this part is the Doctrine of Moses Amyraut lately Professor in the Academy of Saumur in the Treatise on the free choice of man, p. 61. & following. Where first he distinguishes a twofold motion of the will. One which is not indeed separated from that knowledge which draws its origin from reason, but is yet of such a kind that the knowledge from which it is born and blossoms, has not itself arisen from previous consultation: the other which not only is joined with some knowledge, but is born from that knowledge which probouleusis, i.e. consultation preceded, & which is nothing else than the Conclusion which is made from deliberation, several objects, namely, being considered and compared among themselves, or one & the same object viewed in different ways, so that the mind balanced for some while hither & thither by the weights of reasons, at length inclines to one side. Then he observes that that motion of the will, which follows no consultation and deliberation of the mind, is again twofold, namely that by one the will is carried to the end, that is, to blessedness and happiness itself; by the other to the means which are thought to lead to that end.
pass_b: Moses Amyraut, until recently professor at the Academy of Saumur, teaches much the same on this point in his treatise On Man's Free Choice (p. 61 and following). He first distinguishes two movements of the will.

One is not cut off from the knowledge that has its source in reason, but the knowledge from which it springs and grows did not itself come out of any prior weighing. The other is not only joined with knowledge but arises from knowledge that consultation (probouleusis) went before. That knowledge is simply the conclusion reached by deliberation, when several objects are considered and compared, or one and the same object is looked at in different ways, so that the mind, swung this way and that for a while by the weight of reasons, finally leans to one side.

Next he observes that the movement of the will that follows no weighing or deliberation by the mind is itself of two kinds. By one the will is carried toward the end, namely happiness and blessedness itself; by the other toward the means thought to lead to that end.

lemmas.gloss: swung by the weight of reasons

choices.why: The image is of a plant flowering from its root; 'springs and grows' keeps the organic metaphor without strain.

notes: Moses Amyraut, De libero hominis arbitrio, p. 61 ff. Probouleusis is Aristotle's term for the deliberation that precedes choice.

sections.title: Amyraut: neither movement belongs to free choice, which needs prior deliberation (prohairesis)
sections.pass_a: But afterwards he shows that neither of those motions pertains to free choice. Not the former, because free choice is that which Aristotle called prohairesis. Now, he says, some probouleusis precedes every prohairesis. But no one consults about that last end, but is carried to it not only necessarily, but also aprobouleutos. Not also the latter, because although that motion differs from the former, it is also equally aprobouleutos with it. Since it is so sudden, so swift, whether arising from some perturbation, or born from the presence of some great & unforeseen and unexpected object it breaks out, that it anticipates all consultation. Whence he gathers that a motion of this kind is indeed hekousion, that is, spontaneous & voluntary, but not prohairetikon, that is, free and elective. And therefore it is rightly wont to be said that the first impulses of our passions are not in our power; since those things alone are in our power about which we take counsel, whether they are by us, either to be used, or omitted: and therefore what run before all deliberation, those we do not judge to be in our power. Whence at length he concludes p. 65. It remains therefore that those things be thought to pertain to our choice about which we can deliberate, and that we say those likewise have proceeded from our free choice about which we have so deliberated, that desire has followed the deliberation & consultation: in which thing we have often said already that prohairesis is situated.
pass_b: Then he shows that neither movement belongs to free choice. Not the first, because free choice is what Aristotle called prohairesis, and as he says, "every prohairesis is preceded by some probouleusis. No one deliberates about that final end; one is carried toward it not only by necessity but without any prior deliberation (aprobouleutos)."

Not the second either: though it differs from the first, it is just as much without prior deliberation. It is so sudden and so quick, whether it comes from some disturbance or bursts out at the sight of something great, unforeseen and unexpected, that it gets ahead of all weighing. He infers that such a movement is indeed hekousion, spontaneous and voluntary, but not prohairetikon, free and elective.

This is why it is rightly said that the first stirrings of our passions are not in our power. Only the things we take counsel about, whether we should take them up or leave them alone, are in our power, and we do not count as in our power what runs ahead of all deliberation.

So at last he concludes (p. 65): "What belongs to our choice, then, must be the things we can deliberate about. And we should say that those things come from our free choice which we have deliberated about in such a way that desire followed the deliberation and weighing. That, as we have often said, is where prohairesis lies."

choices.english: the first stirrings of our passions
choices.why: The scholastic 'first motions' are the involuntary onset of a passion before reason consents; 'first stirrings' renders the idea.

notes: Amyraut, De libero hominis arbitrio, p. 65. The Greek terms (prohairesis, probouleusis, hekousion, prohairetikon) come from Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.

sections.title: Some also exclude the motive or impulsive necessity that God might impose
sections.pass_a: But besides the necessity which is from coaction, from matter, or from sense, or from any other determination of nature, there is a certain necessity which is conceived to arise from some external cause, as from God himself, so moving and impelling the faculty itself, that he imposes a true necessity of acting, that is, takes away from the agent the power of acting otherwise; although he who acts is supposed to act spontaneously, & not unwilling. Which necessity the Schools call motive and impulsive. But there are not lacking among the Reformed, those who think that this necessity also conflicts with human liberty, and who think that with it there can stand no necessity properly so called, which in the Schools is called necessity of the consequent, in opposition to the necessity which is called of the consequence.
pass_b: Beyond the necessity that comes from compulsion, from matter, from sense or from any other settling by nature, there is a necessity thought to come from an outside cause, God himself for instance, moving and driving the faculty in such a way that he lays on it a true necessity of acting. That is, he removes from the agent the power to act otherwise, even though the agent is supposed to act of his own accord and not unwillingly. The schools call this motive or impulsive necessity.

Some among the Reformed think that this necessity too clashes with human freedom. They hold that freedom cannot coexist with any necessity in the proper sense, what the schools call necessity of the consequent, as opposed to necessity of the consequence.

choices.why: The standard scholastic distinction: necessity of the consequent makes the thing itself necessary, necessity of the consequence only makes an inference valid. The paired technical terms are kept.

sections.title: Ames: free choice is free from all necessity as to the exercise of its act, though it acts infallibly under God's ordination
sections.pass_a: This is the opinion of William Ames formerly Theologian in the Academy of Franeker, We, he says, grant free choice, in that which it does to be free from all necessity, so that properly it cannot act necessarily as to the exercise of its act, although in respect of divine ordination it acts certainly & infallibly. In Bellarmine Disarmed tom. 4. book 4. chap. 1.
pass_b: William Ames, formerly theologian at the Academy of Franeker, takes this view. In his Bellarmine Disarmed (volume 4, book 4, chapter 1) he writes: "We grant that free choice, in what it does, is free from all necessity.
"Properly speaking it cannot act by necessity as regards the exercise of its act, even though, with respect to God's ordaining, it acts certainly and infallibly."

lemmas.gloss: as regards the exercise of its act

choices.why: Ordinatio here is God's decree arranging events; 'ordaining' keeps the active sense.

notes: William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus, tom. 4, lib. 4, cap. 1.

sections.title: Baron: the will is not bound by necessity of the consequent nor by any motive necessity from God
sections.pass_a: The same also thinks Rob. Baron formerly Professor in the Academy of Aberdeen in his general Metaphysics accommodated to the use of Theology, where among many other things he asserts these two, First that the will in eliciting its actions is not held, or constrained by necessity absolutely so called, which they call necessity of the consequent. Then that the will, even of fallen man, is held by no motive, or impulsive necessity in respect of God. He also, he says, gave men free choice, and consequently does not wholly take away that faculty, by imposing necessity on it, either by his eternal decree, or by temporary motion, & inflection. Sect. 12. Disp. 1. on liberty of Choice num. 17.
pass_b: Robert Baron, formerly professor at the Academy of Aberdeen, holds the same in his General Metaphysics Adapted to the Use of Theology. Among much else he makes two claims there.

First, the will is not held or bound, in producing its acts, by necessity in the absolute sense, what they call necessity of the consequent. Second, the will, even of fallen man, is not held by any motive or impulsive necessity with respect to God.

"He too," Baron says, "gave men free choice. So he does not do away with that faculty entirely by laying necessity on it, either through his eternal decree or through a motion and bending in time." (Section 12, Disputation 1, On Freedom of Choice, number 17.)

lemmas.gloss: a motion and bending in time

choices.why: Inflexio is God's turning or bending of the will in time, as opposed to his eternal decree; 'bending' keeps the physical image.

notes: Robert Baron, Metaphysica generalis, sect. 12, disp. 1, De libertate arbitrii, num. 17.

sections.title: Le Blanc: the first view does not really differ from the second, only states it less distinctly
sections.pass_a: But that I may also open what seems to me, I think that the first opinion which defines liberty immunity from coaction in one who acts from the judgement of reason, does not in reality differ from the second opinion, which opposes liberty not only to coaction, but also to the necessity which arises from matter or from sense, which others call Physical necessity. For since it states that immunity from coaction is not worthy of the name of liberty, except in one who uses reason; it evidently supposes that for liberty it is required, that the agent follow the judgement of reason, and not be determined by matter, or by sense. And so this second opinion does not differ from the former, except that it is proposed more distinctly & more explicitly.
pass_b: To give my own view as well: I think the first opinion, which defines freedom as exemption from compulsion in an agent acting on reason's judgement, does not differ in substance from the second, which opposes freedom not only to compulsion but also to the necessity that comes from matter or sense, called by some physical necessity.

The first opinion holds that exemption from compulsion does not deserve the name of freedom except in a being that uses reason. Plainly, then, it assumes that freedom requires the agent to follow reason's judgement and not to be settled by matter or sense. So the second opinion differs from the first only in being stated more precisely and more fully.

choices.why: The pair of comparatives describes a clearer and more developed statement; plain English comparatives give the sense.

sections.title: Both views wrongly confuse the free with the voluntary
sections.pass_a: But in both there is this inconvenience that they altogether confound the free & the voluntary, & state all acts of the will to be free. For according to the common sense of men, & the received use of speaking, that alone is said to be free to us, which is in our power, which can be otherwise, & about which it is permitted to us to consult & deliberate. Now, as we showed above, there are certain acts of the will, to which it is so determined by nature, that they can in no way be otherwise, & about which no deliberation can be set up. Add that all acts which proceed freely from us can be subject to certain precepts, & be commanded, or forbidden by some divine, or human law. But this in no way suits those acts about which the will holds itself plainly immutably, so that in no state could it, or can it ever act otherwise. Finally since those with whom we have to do, confess & acknowledge that there is a great difference between acts of the will, namely that some are so in our power, that we can consult & deliberate about them; and either do, or omit them according to the various judgement of the practical mind, or even do the contrary; but that of others the nature is plainly different; why will they not mark things distinct by nature, with distinct words also, & according to the use received in the Schools appropriate to those indeed the name of free, but to these of voluntary? since it is the part of a wise man not to depart without necessity from the common mode of speaking.
pass_b: Both views share one drawback: they wholly confuse the free with the voluntary and hold that every act of the will is free. In the common understanding of men and in ordinary usage, we call free only what is in our power, what could be otherwise, and what we are allowed to weigh and deliberate about.

But as shown above, there are acts of the will to which it is so fixed by nature that they cannot be otherwise in any way, and about which no deliberation can be held. Further, every act that comes from us freely can fall under precepts and be commanded or forbidden by some law, divine or human. That does not fit at all the acts toward which the will stands quite unchangeably, so that in no state could it, or ever can it, act otherwise.

Lastly, the men we are dealing with admit a great difference among the will's acts. Some are in our power, so that we can weigh and deliberate about them and, as the practical mind judges one way or another, do them, leave them undone, or even do the opposite; the others are of a quite different kind. Why, then, will they not give things that differ in nature different names too, and, following the usage of the schools, reserve 'free' for the first and 'voluntary' for the second? A wise man does not leave the common way of speaking without need.

choices.english: the men we are dealing with
choices.why: The idiom names one's opponents in a dispute; here the Reformed writers just discussed.
rejected: those with whom we have business

sections.title: Some distinguish free choice broadly taken (intellectual spontaneity) from free choice strictly taken
sections.pass_a: But among those Learned men who seem to confound the free & the voluntary, there are some who advise that the liberty of the will, or free Choice is taken in a twofold manner, broadly, namely, & strictly. Liberty of the will in general, or broadly taken, according to them, is nothing else than to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, the spontaneous with the light, or judgement of the intellect going before. And so in this properly consists that general liberty of the will, that the will so far has Dominion of its act, that it can by no means be coerced, but at pleasure, from a certain reason, consideration, or judgement, moves itself, & restrains itself, acts, or does not act.
pass_b: Among the learned men who seem to confuse the free and the voluntary, some point out that freedom of the will, or free choice, is taken in two ways, a broad one and a strict one.

Freedom of the will in general, or in the broad sense, is for them nothing but to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, spontaneity led by the light or judgement of the intellect. This general freedom of the will properly consists in the will's having mastery over its act to the extent that it can never be forced. Instead it moves or restrains itself, acts or refrains, as it pleases, for some definite reason, consideration or judgement.

choices.why: Pro libito means at one's discretion; it is qualified at once by 'for some definite reason', so it does not mean caprice.

sections.title: On their view this broad freedom is exercised even toward the last end, and natural necessity does not lessen it
sections.pass_a: This is that liberty, which according to their opinion, the will exercises in all its actions, and that not only when it is occupied about means looking to the end, or those things which conduce little, or nothing to the end, but also, when it is occupied about the end itself. And therefore the very necessity which follows the nature of the will, and is agreeable to it, & by which it is determined to pursue the highest end, by no means overturns, or diminishes this liberty of the will.
pass_b: This, in their view, is the freedom the will exercises in all its acts. It does so not only when dealing with the means to the end, or with things that contribute little or nothing to the end, but also when dealing with the end itself.
So the necessity that flows from the will's nature and agrees with it, by which the will is set on pursuing the highest end, in no way destroys or lessens this freedom of the will.

choices.english: in no way destroys or lessens
choices.why: Minime is an emphatic negative; 'in no way' keeps both the negation and its force.

sections.title: Strict free choice concerns means and what is in our power, and includes indifference
sections.pass_a: But liberty used more strictly, or free choice is restricted, by their own admission to means related to the end, or to those things which conduce little, or nothing to the end, & is occupied about ta eph' hemin, that is, about those things which are in our power, & is rightly defined by Aristotle the spontaneous arisen from previous deliberation, or Deliberative appetition of those things which are in our power. In which sense those acts are called free which are merely contingent, & which can be done by us at our choice, or not be done. And in that respect liberty includes a certain indifference, nor is the will otherwise free than inasmuch as it is indifferent, namely, since it can act about the same object, or not act, & since it can choose as well this, as another, or its opposite. And in this sense God does not love himself freely, because by necessity of nature he wills & loves himself; nor also does man freely will to be happy, & not will to be miserable, because he so wills & not otherwise by a certain natural necessity.
pass_b: Freedom in the stricter sense, or free choice, is by their own admission limited to means directed to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to it. It concerns ta eph' hemin, the things in our power, and Aristotle rightly defines it as the spontaneous arising from prior deliberation, or deliberative desire for things in our power.

In this sense acts are called free when they are purely contingent and we can do them or not do them as we choose. Taken so, freedom includes a kind of indifference. The will is free only in so far as it is indifferent, that is, able to act or not act toward the same object, and able to choose this, or something else, or its opposite.

In this sense God does not love himself freely, since he wills and loves himself by the necessity of his nature. Nor does man freely want to be happy and not want to be miserable, since he wills this, and cannot will otherwise, by a natural necessity.

lemmas.gloss: ta eph' hemin, the things in our power

choices.why: The technical term for the will's openness to either alternative is kept, as in the earlier theses.

notes: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.3, defines choice as deliberate desire of things in our power.

sections.title: Strang and Alexander More likewise distinguish free choice broadly and strictly taken
sections.pass_a: This is the doctrine of John Strang, Doctor of S. S. Theology & primary Professor in the Academy of Glasgow, in the Treatise on the will & actions of God about sin, book 3. chap. 14. Where after he has expounded & drawn out more widely these things which we have said, he says he does not deny that the word free choice is rightly used in that strict sense, although in another & wider sense he affirms all actions of the will to be free. And in a similar manner also the most Celebrated Alexander More distinguishes free choice, On Grace & free Choice Disp. 1. Thesis 28. Where he proposes two definitions, one of free choice more widely taken, the other of free choice strictly taken. According to the former notion free choice is described by him, The endowment most proper to an intelligent nature by which it wills nothing, or shuns, except what it has understood to be good, or evil. But according to the latter, the will inasmuch as it chooses the means shown by the intellect after consultation.
pass_b: This is the teaching of John Strang, Doctor of Sacred Theology and principal professor at the Academy of Glasgow, in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin (book 3, chapter 14). After setting out and developing what we have described, he says he does not deny that the term free choice is rightly used in that strict sense, though in another and wider sense he maintains that all the will's acts are free.

The famous Alexander More draws the same kind of distinction in his On Grace and Free Choice (disputation 1, thesis 28). He offers two definitions, one of free choice in the wider sense and one of free choice in the strict sense.

In the first sense he describes free choice as "the endowment most proper to an intelligent nature, by which it wills or shuns nothing except what it has understood to be good or evil." In the second, it is "the will as it chooses means set before it by the intellect after deliberation."

choices.why: Strang was principal of Glasgow; 'principal professor' renders professor primarius without assuming the later title.

notes: John Strang, De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3, cap. 14; Alexander More, De gratia et libero arbitrio, disp. 1, thesis 28.
